content: The MeltPro assay was included in this review, but no independent evaluations of the technology were identified. The Xpert MTB/XDR assay operates on Cepheid’s GeneXpert platform, similar to the Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assays. However, the MTB/XDR assay utilizes a 10-color multiplexing technology, which is an advancement over the 6-color technology used in the MTB/RIF and MTB/RIF Ultra assays. According to the manufacturer, the Xpert MTB/XDR assay is designed as a reflex test for specimens (either unprocessed sputum or concentrated sputum sediments) that have already tested positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC). The manufacturer also notes that specimens with “MTB trace detected” results from the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay are likely below the detection limit of the MTB/XDR assay and are not recommended for testing with the MTB/XDR assay. Similar to the MTB/RIF and Ultra assays, the MTB/XDR assay detects both live and dead bacteria. Results are reported as either “MTB not detected” or “MTB detected.” If MTB is detected, the assay provides results for drug resistance, indicating whether resistance to specific drugs is “detected” or “not detected.” If the results are “MTB not detected,” “invalid,” “error,” or “no result,” no drug susceptibility testing (DST) results are reported. Kanamycin and capreomycin are no longer recommended for the treatment of multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) in longer treatment regimens, as per conditional recommendations with very low certainty in the evidence. The World Health Organization (WHO) consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis diagnostics emphasize the use of rapid diagnostic tools for TB detection and drug resistance testing. The Xpert MTB/XDR assay targets specific drug-resistance-associated gene regions. For isoniazid resistance, it detects mutations in the inhA promoter, katG, and other regions. For ethionamide resistance, it also targets the inhA promoter. Fluoroquinolone resistance is identified through mutations in gyrA and gyrB. Resistance to amikacin, capreomycin, and kanamycin is detected through mutations in the rrs gene and the eis promoter. The WHO Global TB Programme initiated a systematic review to update guidelines on the use of low-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for detecting resistance to isoniazid and second-line TB drugs in individuals with TB symptoms. The review addressed specific questions (PICO framework) comparing low-complexity automated NAATs to culture-based phenotypic DST or genotypic sequencing for detecting resistance to isoniazid, fluoroquinolones, ethionamide, and amikacin. For isoniazid resistance detection, three multinational studies involving 1,605 participants were analyzed. The sensitivity ranged from 81% to 100%, and specificity ranged from 87% to 100%. However, concerns about indirectness in study populations and variability in mutations between mono-resistant and MDR strains led to moderate certainty ratings for both sensitivity and specificity. For fluoroquinolone resistance detection, three multinational studies with 1,337 participants were included. Sensitivity ranged from 83% to 100%, while specificity ranged from 84% to 100%. Inconsistencies in specificity estimates led to moderate certainty for specificity and high certainty for sensitivity. For ethionamide resistance detection, one multinational study with 434 participants was analyzed. Sensitivity ranged from 78% to 100%, and specificity ranged from 97% to 100%. Due to risk of bias and imprecision, the evidence was rated as very low certainty for both sensitivity and specificity. For amikacin resistance detection, one multinational study with 490 participants was included. Sensitivity ranged from 75% to 95%, and specificity ranged from 96% to 100%. The evidence was rated as low certainty for sensitivity and high certainty for specificity due to imprecision and limited participant data. A cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted to evaluate the affordability and economic impact of implementing low-complexity automated NAATs. Two assays were identified: MeltPro MTB/RIF and Xpert MTB/XDR. However, no published studies provided direct evidence on the cost or cost-effectiveness of these assays. The Xpert MTB/XDR assay requires upgrading to 10-color GeneXpert modules, with costs ranging from $3,860 for module conversion to $72,350 for a new 16-module system. Additional costs include repeat testing for indeterminate results and operational expenses. The assay’s rapid turnaround time (<90 minutes) may improve treatment initiation, reduce loss to follow-up, and enhance survival rates, potentially offsetting costs in the long term. The introduction of Xpert MTB/XDR is expected to improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce delays in detecting drug resistance. However, the lack of transmission modeling studies limits understanding of its long-term population-level impact. Identifying more cases earlier could reduce ongoing transmission and lead to cost savings over time. End-user perspectives highlight the value of low-complexity automated NAATs for their speed, accuracy, and ability to detect drug resistance. Laboratory technicians appreciate the ease of use and biosafety improvements compared to sputum microscopy. However, successful implementation requires adequate training for clinicians and laboratory staff, as well as clear guidelines and algorithms to support result interpretation and communication. Sustainable funding and efficient sample transportation systems are also critical for feasibility.
